description: Iridium is a chemical element with symbol Ir and atomic number 77. It is a very hard, brittle, silvery-white transition metal of the platinum group, considered the second-densest naturally occurring metal after osmium with a density of 22.56 g/cm³. It is one of the most corrosion-resistant metals, remaining resistant even at temperatures as high as 2,000 °C.
uses: The dominant uses of iridium and its alloys are in high-performance spark plugs, crucibles for recrystallization of semiconductors at high temperatures, and electrodes for the production of chlorine in the chloralkali process. Important compounds of iridium are chlorides and iodides in industrial catalysis, and iridium is a component of some OLEDs. The radioisotope iridium-192 finds application in brachytherapy and industrial radiography for nondestructive testing of welds.
characteristics: Iridium is white with a slight yellowish cast, extremely brittle and hard, with a very high melting point and the 10th highest boiling point among all elements. It is the only metal to maintain good mechanical properties in air at temperatures above 1,600 °C and becomes a superconductor below 0.14 K. Iridium has the second-highest modulus of elasticity among metals and is the most corrosion-resistant metal known, not attacked by acids including aqua regia.
